claims.text: A machine-learning framework integrating high-throughput experimental and computational databases can rapidly identify optimized RHEA compositions.
Mixing entropy, atomic-size difference, and valence-electron concentration are suitable tailored descriptors for this RHEA-design framework.
The proposed framework can optimize intrinsic strength, ductility, and weight simultaneously.
RHEAs consist of multiple principal refractory elements forming a random solid solution.
The stated RHEA initial state has high configurational entropy.
A data-driven machine-learning model trained on high-throughput data can screen the vast RHEA compositional space using physicochemical descriptors.
The intended alloys operate under high-temperature refractory conditions requiring maintenance of structural integrity and performance.
Controlled atomic-size mismatch and chemical ordering can engineer lattice distortion and phase stability.
Engineered lattice distortion and phase stability mediate dislocation behavior and mechanical resistance.
The machine-learning framework statistically correlates selected descriptors with mechanical properties and density.
The framework can predict compositions that balance dislocation impediment and resulting strength with microstructural ductility.
The framework can minimize alloy density while retaining the targeted mechanical properties.
Machine-learning-designed RHEAs will have higher strength and ductility and lower weight than alloys optimized by conventional thermo-kinetic and simulation strategies.
Traditional alloy-design methods include thermodynamic analysis, ab initio simulation, and experimental trials.
The success of the approach depends on the quality and diversity of its training dataset.
Predictions may be less reliable for compositions outside the domain represented by the available data.
The magnitude of improvement and generalizability across the full compositional space remain uncertain pending extensive experimental validation.
